title: The wudu verse
hook: wash your face, your hands to the elbows, wipe your head, wash your feet (5:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, halal, the food of the People of the Book, lawful both ways. Your line was a shared table. Did you invite someone, or say yes to an invitation? Day three hundred ninety-one.

Before prayer, in bathrooms, courtyards and airport washrooms all over the world, Muslims stand at a tap and go through the same quiet sequence. Hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, ears, feet. A stranger watching might think it's just hygiene, and it is clean. But it's also something else: a passage from the ordinary into prayer. Back in year one, we learned the word wudu. Today, the verse that sets it down.
screen: `AT A TAP, BEFORE PRAYER.` → `HANDS, FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` → `THE VERSE THAT SETS IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Al-Ma'idah 6, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and (wash) your feet up to the ankles." That's the core, four actions, in the order the verse names them: wash the face, wash the arms to the elbows, wipe the head, and the feet. The rinsing of mouth and nose, the ears, the repeating of each part, come from the Prophet's own practice, described in the hadith. Here's a detail worth knowing. The Arabic word for your feet can be read with two different vowel endings, and both readings are old and recognized. Read one way, the feet belong with the things you wash. Read the other way, they belong with the head, which you wipe. Sunni Muslims wash the feet; most Shia Muslims wipe them. Same verse, two faithful readings. Then the verse makes room for difficulty. If you're ill, or traveling, or can't find water, use clean earth: tayammum, a light touch of the hands on clean soil, then over face and hands. And it ends by saying God doesn't want to make things hard for you; He wants to purify you and complete His favor on you, so that you might be grateful. A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the inner side: when a believer washes the face, every wrong the eyes looked at leaves with the water, until he comes out clean. So the washing is written, step by step. And what it washes is more than skin.
screen: `FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET` · `WASHED OR WIPED: TWO READINGS` · `NO WATER: CLEAN EARTH` · `WHAT LEAVES WITH THE WATER` · then, large: `WHEN YE RISE UP FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: If you make wudu, make your next one with this verse in mind: say it to yourself, step by step, face, arms, head, feet. If you don't, try washing your hands and face slowly once today, as a small passage from one part of the day to another. For now, when the bell starts, picture water running over your hands. Then your face. Let one thing you'd like to leave behind from today, a sharp word, a glance, a worry, run off with it. The bell holds the time.

Wudu, the washing before prayer, from a root meaning brightness and cleanness. Al-Ma'idah 6: wash the face, the arms to the elbows, wipe the head, and the feet; and if there's no water, clean earth. Today's word.
Your line: the washing, written. Today, at one washing, slow down and remember that the steps are written in the Qur'an, and what they're meant to carry away. Day three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Before prayer, Muslims perform wudu: washing the hands, mouth, nose, face and arms, wiping the head and ears, and washing the feet (Sunni) or wiping them (most Shia); when water can't be used, they perform tayammum with clean earth.

match.prompt: the wudu verse — tap the pairs.
pairs: washed by Sunnis, wiped by most Shia
clean earth when there's no water

myth: every detail of wudu is spelled out in 5:6
the verse names the core; rinsing the mouth, nose and ears comes from the Prophet's practice.
the word for feet in 5:6 has two old recognized readings
one groups the feet with washing, the other with wiping.
the verse gives tayammum, with clean earth.

fork.setup: you're traveling, it's time to pray, and there's no water anywhere. what does 5:6 say?
options: skip the prayer until you find water.
use clean earth: tayammum, on the face and hands.
fork.reveal: tayammum with clean earth. the verse adds that God doesn't want to make things hard for you.

original.note: Arabic: wudu, the washing before prayer, from a root meaning brightness and cleanness.

trapdoor: what you thought: washing before prayer is just hygiene.
what it means: a sequence written in the Qur'an, face, arms, head, feet, a passage from the ordinary into prayer.
what a scholar hears: the two qira'at of arjulakum/arjulikum behind washing or wiping the feet; and tayammum in the same verse.
recall: a greeting, a wish for life
a trust: anything placed in your care

Hook refers back to the year-one lesson on wudu (y1 day 13 teaches it).
Hook softened from 'five times a day' to 'before prayer', since one wudu can serve several prayers until it is broken.

Whether the order of the steps (tartib) is obligatory is debated (required for Shafi'is and Hanbalis, a sunnah for Hanafis and Malikis); the teach now says 'in the order the verse names them' without ruling. Confirm.
Wiping the feet is Twelver (Ja'fari) practice; Zaydi Shia wash them. Script now says 'most Shia'. Confirm.
